newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada begins new consultations on Zaire rescue.
newsitem.headline: Canada begins new consultations on Zaire rescue.

text.p: Canada began consulting its allies on Monday on whether to send a military force to help refugees in eastern Zaire after an inconclusive weekend planning meeting in Stuttgart.
Officials acknowledged their mounting frustration that four international meetings over the past 11 days had not been enough to get the humanitarian rescue mission off the ground.
But they pointed out the difficulties of getting international agreement on how to proceed in the face of a changing situation on the ground.

"Any mission that would go would have to be an international coalition, and right now we're consulting to see what the various countries are prepared to do," Catherine Lappe, spokeswoman for Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, said.
The Canadian government's approach was three-pronged.

Axworthy was busy calling other foreign ministers, Defence Minister Doug Young was meeting U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry in Washington, and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien had a word with President Bill Clinton during an Asia-Pacific summit in the Philippines.

Chretien, who assembled international support for a mission two weeks ago, before the return of half a million refugees to Rwanda from Zaire changed the picture, still appeared to be leaning toward sending a scaled-down force.
"My view is we have to be ready for a military intervention," he told a Manila news conference. "We are not sure how much of it is needed."
Young said last week that a new meeting would be required to make the final decision, but officials since then have said it might be possible to arrive at a consensus by phone.

The U.N. Security Council specifically authorised a force on Nov. 15 to help refugees return and provide corridors for aid to reach both refugees and those Zairians who have been displaced by fighting in their country.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said in Brussels that the world was dragging its feet because it did not care about Africa.
"I am frankly shocked when I see that kind of apathy hiding behind endless discussions," he told reporters.

Young said in Washington: "The situation is still somewhat confused on the ground. There has been some movement, we're told, even in the last 24 hours, moving towards a crossing area at Goma from the southern part of Eastern Zaire."
Most of the refugees that headed home to Rwanda crossed through Goma, but aid agencies have said hundreds of thousands remain in the southern area to which Young was referring.
"Whether or not we have to do something militarily in the traditional sense of peacekeeping or humanitarian aid support is difficult to tell at this point," he told reporters.
Besides the Nov. 15 Security Council meeting, diplomats met in New York on Wednesday, military planners met Friday through Sunday in Stuttgart, and aid officials met in Geneva on Saturday.

The long-awaited meeting in Stuttgart set out various scenarios but did not settle on any or where the mission would be based. Rwanda says a military force would be unwelcome, leading to speculation Uganda might be chosen as a base.
